issues.detail: Hebrew 'בְּֽנֵי אָדָ֗ם' means 'sons of men' (i.e., people/humans), but Chinese renders it as '發熱的人' (feverish people), which is not the meaning. The Hebrew word 'לֹהֲטִים' is a participle meaning 'burning' or 'blazing' (referring to the lions in the previous phrase), not 'feverish people'. The phrase 'בְּֽנֵי אָדָ֗ם' is a separate construct phrase meaning 'sons of men' and is not connected to 'לֹהֲטִים' as 'feverish people'. The Chinese translation conflates and misrenders this, changing the meaning.
Hebrew 'שִׁנֵּיהֶם' means 'their teeth', but Chinese renders it as '他們的象牙' (their ivory). 'Ivory' is not in the Hebrew text; it is an addition that changes the image from teeth to ivory tusks.
